posts.title: Why everyone loves dividend?
posts.text: I’ve heard of dividends long before I decided to learn about stock market, it seems like many people prefer divdend-paying stock. So it’s naturally to raise this question: what are dividends and why everyone loves them? DefinitionAccording to wiki, dividends are periodic payments made to shareholders from corporate profits. Reflected in the stock market, there are two kinds of distribution of dividends. Cash dividends. Pretty self-explanatory, we get cash. Stock dividends. Also self-explanatory, we get stocks. If that’s the only change, of course everyone loves them. However, when dividends happen, the stock price would fall proportionally. Take cash dividends as an example: suppose you have 10 shares at $10 each, and the genuine company decides to pay a dividend of $5 per share (seems too genuine), then you get $50 cash and 10 shares at $5 each. The asset value before and after cash dividends doesn’t change at all! For now, we leave this question for a while and we will come back to this topic in later chapters. ProcedureDuring a dividend payment procedure, there are 3 important dates. Record date. This is when the company records who can get the dividends. Every shareholder at this date can get dividends. Those who buy after this date can’t. Ex-Dividend date. This is when the stock price adjusts (minus dividend amount). Payment date. This is when people get paid in cash or in stocks. Apart from these dates, we also need to know about Dividend Tax, which charges from dividend amount. Usually, in order to encourage shareholders to invest for longer time, dividend tax get lower when people hold stocks for a longer period. Dividend advantagesBack to the previous question: since the asset value remains the same, what’s the meaning of getting dividends? After reviewing materials and continuous thinking, I think we can understand it from these perspectives. Dividends vs. Capital Gains: A Fundamental DifferenceIs the market capitalization of a company reflecting the overall asset value? No. The market capitalization is a valuation of a company, no matter how much asset this company has right now (we use PB to describe this relation, PB=$\frac{market\quad cap}{asset}$). For good companies, their market capitalization is higher than their asset (PB>1). Shareholders are owners of a company. Let’s get back to the example. If you sell 5 shares of the company at $10 each, you get $50 cash and your shareholding drops 50%, the stock price remains. If you get $5 cash dividends per share, you still get $50 cash and your shareholding remains, the stock price drops 50%. You see, the difference between them is whether shareholding drops or stock price drops. This difference is fundamental and crucial. Stock price is a valuation of a company and it’s of course important, but it’s not actual value of the company. The decrease of a stock price only means the valuation of it decreases. You still hold the exact shareholding of that company, and your $50 cash is paid by that company from its profits. It’s not an expectation or valuation or whatsoerver, it’s hard cash. The valuation can fluctuate, but your shareholding can’t. So it’s possible that you get $50 cash dividens every year, but you can’t sell 5 shares every year (10 shares can only last for 2 years). Don’t Forget Post-Dividend Price RecoveryAlways remember, stock price is only a valuation. After the ex-dividend date, the stock price drops, but it may recovery within a period of time, because the fundamentals of the company remain unchanged. However, not every company can recovery or bounce back in a short time, it depends on the fundamentals of that company. What I am saying is paying dividends doesn’t change how we value a company, and its stock price would get to a point where it should be. So, if you hold a stock for a sufficient long time and get dividends frequently, you may get a negative cost basis where you get more dividends than your principal. So, get back to our title, the more precise statement should be: every long-term investors love dividends. Short-term investors may hate them because they cause the stock price to drop. No matter what strategies you pick, knowing deeper about dividends is always necessary.
